coke-reports-1777-vol5:
The fifth volume of Wilson's 1777 Reports continues Coke's monumental record of decided cases. Coke reported the law of the courts of Elizabeth and James while that law was still being made. By Wilson's time, the Reports were old, authoritative, and still in daily use.

The cases in this volume keep returning to the same great theme: the common law defended against claims of royal prerogative. Coke's learning fills the margins, tying each new decision to centuries of precedent. His courage shows too, for he reported rulings that had put him at odds with the king he served. Generations of lawyers learned their craft from these pages. The volume helps explain why Coke became the patron saint of English liberty in the eyes of later ages.
degroot-religious-system-china-vol5:
Volume Five of de Groot's great work, from 1907, follows the sacred year. Festivals, processions, and temple fairs fill this part of the system. China's religion steps out of books and into the streets here.

Season by season, gods are feasted, paraded, and thanked in public. Drums, incense, opera, and crowds mark the great days de Groot describes. He shows faith as a whole town acts it, not just reads it. The panorama catches belief in motion across one full year. Few volumes in the set feel so alive or so full of noise and color. De Groot lets the crowd, not just the priest, carry the story.
lamb-works-lucas-vol5:
Lucas printed the Lambs' letters from 1796 to 1820 as the fifth volume of the 1903 Works. In his notes he thanks owners who lent new letters found even while the volumes were in press. One joint letter to young Louisa Martin, dated March 28, 1809, has Mary start and Charles take over in a playful mood.

Gossip, book talk, jokes, and warm feeling run through the letters to friends like Coleridge, Wordsworth, and Hazlitt. Charles writes as freely here as in any Elia essay, often more freely. For readers who love Elia, the volume gives that same voice at its most open and unguarded.
las-casas-historia-indias-vol5:
Volume 5 closes Las Casas's vast Historia de las Indias, in the 1875 printing. The friar carries his lifelong fight for Native rights to its end. Five volumes of proof, argument, and moral fury come to a close.

Late campaigns, laws, and debates fill the final stretch of the work. Las Casas never softens his charge that Spain ruined the Indies. He pleads, warns, and accuses in the voice of an old prophet. Readers feel a whole long life spent on one great cause. The Apostle of the Indies rests his case, and later ages judge it.
middleton-works-dyce-1840-vol5:
The fifth volume of Dyce's Works of Thomas Middleton, from 1840, completes the first collected edition. Dyce closes the set with the remaining pieces and the apparatus a scholar needs. Middleton's modern reputation begins with these five volumes on the shelf.

Beyond the famous tragedies and comedies, Middleton wrote masques, pageants, and prose pieces for the city he served as chronologer. The closing volume gathers what the earlier ones could not hold. Dyce adds corrections and an index to the whole work. Later editors have revised his texts, but theatre companies still start from the revival Dyce made possible in 1840.
